doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Identifying Nat and Cannonball Adderley in a listening test
summary: Gardner recognises a later Adderley quintet recording from Nat's cornet tone and Cannonball's high register.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Yeah. It would be unlikely these days. Well sometimes I like to play a tune for folks and get their take on it. So of all the things, the myriad of things I could pick, I’m going to try this out on you and see what you think.
From what you said it sounds like something your father would have liked.
The title tune that’s being played and the instrumentation already narrows it down to essentially a few people. Okay. I’m going to take a stab at this.
This is one of the later versions of Cannonball Adderley’s Quintet.
Yeah. I say later because he’s doing some things in there that I have never heard him doing back in the earlier versions of that quintet. He sounds like this is from the early seventies I’m guessing.
Well this is from the “Mercy Mercy” LP. And it’s a Nat composition.
Yeah, yeah. Okay. That’s definitely Nat. I knew that from the first couple of notes.
Well I’m a trumpet player, you know?

I know but it’s so funny you say that because the guys that I was fortunate enough to talk to, like Sweets Edison and that generation, they make such a thing out of that. Like “in my day you could tell a player in two measures.” Now you just said the same thing. Can you put it into words? Or maybe —

Well with Nat I would have to say it’s — well the dead giveaway would be his tone. Because he is playing cornet, and the cornet is strikingly different than the trumpet. Most trumpeters can hear the difference right off you know. The cornet has a much mellower sound, and he’s — well I was going to say he’s playing it like a trumpet. I mean he’s playing it like a trumpeter would play a trumpet, you know? And all that stuff that he’s — and then beyond that, beyond the sound of the horn, you have all these Natisms that are his congregation of notes. But the same thing — I was able to tell the same thing with Cannonball much later when he went up into the high register and, what is it, and © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

distorted the notes when he went up into the higher register, and then a run that he did where it was his full tone [scats] but it was just a full huge tone, and it felt like he was blowing the brass off the horn. And I said, oh that’s Cannonball. I know that. That’s Cannon. Now the saxophonist like yourself, I’m sure you’d be able to —

Oh yeah. You’d be able to tell from the first couple of notes you know, oh that’s Cannonball. And in the beginning of that he was doing some non-Cannonballish things, to my ears, just because of my lack of knowledge of this part of Cannonball’s playing. But as it went on, that’s when I said okay, that’s Cannonball, yeah.
